## email.dkim.missing

**DKIM key not found** · passive · default severity **medium**

A configured DKIM selector publishes no usable key at &lt;selector&gt;._domainkey, so signatures made with it fail verification. Selectors can't be discovered from DNS: without configured selectors Seta only tries common names, and finding none there doesn't mean the domain lacks DKIM.

**How to fix:** Publish the public key your mail provider gives you at &lt;selector&gt;._domainkey.&lt;domain&gt;, or remove the selector from the configuration if it's no longer used.

**References:**

- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6376#section-3.6.2>

## email.dkim.weak_key

**DKIM RSA key is too short** · passive · default severity **high**

A DKIM selector publishes an RSA key shorter than 2048 bits. 1024-bit keys are considered breakable by well-resourced attackers, and anything shorter can be factored cheaply, letting anyone forge signatures for the domain.

**How to fix:** Generate a 2048-bit key with your mail provider, publish it under a new selector, switch signing to it, then revoke the old selector.

**References:**

- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8301#section-3.2>

## email.dmarc.external_auth

**External DMARC report destination is not authorized** · passive · default severity **medium**

The DMARC record sends reports to a mailbox in another organization's domain, but that domain does not publish the authorization record receivers check before sending (&lt;domain&gt;._report._dmarc.&lt;destination&gt;). Receivers silently drop those reports.

**How to fix:** Ask the report destination (or your DMARC vendor) to publish "&lt;your-domain&gt;._report._dmarc.&lt;their-domain&gt; TXT v=DMARC1", or send reports to your own domain.

**References:**

- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7489#section-7.1>

## email.dmarc.missing

**No DMARC record** · passive · default severity **high**

Neither the domain nor its organizational domain publishes a DMARC record at _dmarc. Receivers apply no policy to mail that fails SPF and DKIM alignment, and you get no reports about who sends mail as your domain.

**How to fix:** Publish a TXT record at _dmarc, starting with "v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:dmarc@&lt;domain&gt;" and moving to p=quarantine or p=reject once reports show legitimate mail passes.

**References:**

- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7489>

## email.dmarc.no_reporting

**DMARC aggregate reporting is not configured** · passive · default severity **low**

The DMARC record has no rua= address, so you never learn which servers send mail as your domain or whether legitimate mail fails authentication. Without reports it's unsafe to tighten the policy.

**How to fix:** Add rua=mailto:&lt;address&gt; to the DMARC record, or point it at a DMARC report processor.

**References:**

- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7489#section-7.2>

## email.dmarc.policy_none

**DMARC policy is p=none** · passive · default severity **medium**

The DMARC policy only monitors: receivers deliver mail that fails authentication as if there were no DMARC at all. p=none is meant as a short first step, but often stays forever.

**How to fix:** Review aggregate reports, make sure legitimate senders pass, then move to p=quarantine and finally p=reject.

**References:**

- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7489#section-6.3>
- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7489#section-6.7>

## email.dmarc.syntax

**Invalid DMARC record** · passive · default severity **high**

The DMARC record is malformed, or more than one is published. Receivers then ignore DMARC for the domain entirely.

**How to fix:** Publish exactly one record starting with "v=DMARC1;" and a valid p= tag.

**References:**

- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7489#section-6.3>
- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7489#section-6.6.3>

## email.dnsbl.listed

**Mail server is on a DNS blocklist** · passive · default severity **high**

An IPv4 address of an MX host appears on a DNS blocklist. MX hosts usually also send mail, and receivers consult these lists to reject or junk mail from listed addresses.

**How to fix:** Find out why the address was listed (compromised account, open relay, shared IP reputation), fix the cause, then request delisting on the blocklist's website.

**References:**

- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5782>
- <https://www.spamcop.net/bl.shtml>
- <https://psbl.org/>
- <https://docs.spamhaustech.com/40-real-world-usage/DQS/000-intro.html>

## email.mtasts.invalid

**MTA-STS policy is broken** · passive · default severity **medium**

The domain announces MTA-STS but the record or policy is invalid, the policy can't be fetched over valid HTTPS, or the policy doesn't cover every MX host. In enforce mode, senders refuse to deliver to MX hosts the policy doesn't list.

**How to fix:** Serve a valid policy at https://mta-sts.&lt;domain&gt;/.well-known/mta-sts.txt with a publicly trusted certificate, list every MX host under mx:, and bump the id= in the TXT record.

**References:**

- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8461#section-3>
- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8461#section-4.1>

## email.mtasts.missing

**No MTA-STS policy** · passive · default severity **low**

The domain publishes no MTA-STS record at _mta-sts. Without it, senders fall back to opportunistic TLS, which an attacker on the network path can strip to read or alter mail in transit.

**How to fix:** Serve a policy at https://mta-sts.&lt;domain&gt;/.well-known/mta-sts.txt (start with mode: testing) and publish "_mta-sts TXT v=STSv1; id=&lt;timestamp&gt;".

**References:**

- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8461>

## email.mtasts.testing

**MTA-STS policy is in testing mode** · passive · default severity **info**

The MTA-STS policy is in mode: testing, so senders report TLS failures but still deliver over unprotected connections.

**How to fix:** Once TLS-RPT reports show no failures, switch the policy to mode: enforce and bump the id= in the TXT record.

**References:**

- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8461#section-5>

## email.mx.fcrdns

**MX host lacks forward-confirmed reverse DNS** · passive · default severity **low**

An address of an MX host has no PTR record, or its PTR names don't resolve back to the same address. Many receivers penalize or reject mail from servers without forward-confirmed reverse DNS, and MX hosts usually send mail too.

**How to fix:** Ask the owner of the IP range (your hosting provider) to set a PTR record for each MX address that names a host resolving back to that address.

**References:**

- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8601#section-2.7.3>
- <https://support.google.com/a/answer/81126>

## email.mx.missing

**No MX records** · passive · default severity **high**

The domain publishes no MX records. Senders then fall back to the domain's A/AAAA records (the "implicit MX" of RFC 5321), which is rarely intended: mail is either delivered to a web server or bounces after retrying for days. Domains that do not receive mail should say so explicitly with a null MX record (RFC 7505).

**How to fix:** Publish MX records pointing at your mail servers. If the domain does not receive mail, publish a null MX record instead ("@ IN MX 0 .") so senders fail fast.

**References:**

- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5321#section-5.1>
- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7505>

## email.mx.unresolvable

**MX host does not resolve** · passive · default severity **high**

An MX record points at a host name with no A or AAAA records, or at an IP address instead of a host name. Senders cannot deliver to it and fall through to the next MX, or queue and eventually bounce if it is the only one.

**How to fix:** Point the MX record at a host name that has A/AAAA records, or remove the stale MX record.

**References:**

- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5321#section-5.1>
- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2181#section-10.3>

## email.spf.lookup_limit

**SPF exceeds the 10 DNS lookup limit** · passive · default severity **high**

Evaluating the SPF record takes more than 10 DNS-querying terms (include, a, mx, ptr, exists, redirect), counted recursively through includes. Receivers stop at 10 and return a permanent error, so SPF fails for legitimate mail. This usually happens silently when a new SaaS sender is added.

**How to fix:** Remove includes for services you no longer use, replace a/mx terms with ip4/ip6 ranges, or split senders across subdomains.

**References:**

- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7208#section-4.6.4>

## email.spf.missing

**No SPF record** · passive · default severity **high**

The domain publishes no SPF record, so receivers cannot tell which servers may send mail for it. Spoofed mail is more likely to be delivered, and DMARC can only pass via DKIM. Domains that never send mail need a record too, to say so.

**How to fix:** Publish a TXT record listing your senders, e.g. "v=spf1 include:_spf.google.com -all". For a domain that sends no mail, publish "v=spf1 -all".

**References:**

- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7208>

## email.spf.multiple

**Multiple SPF records** · passive · default severity **high**

The domain publishes more than one SPF record. RFC 7208 makes this a permanent error: receivers ignore all of them, as if the domain had no SPF at all.

**How to fix:** Merge the records into a single "v=spf1 ..." TXT record.

**References:**

- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7208#section-4.5>

## email.spf.permissive_all

**SPF allows any sender** · passive · default severity **critical**

The SPF policy authorizes every server on the internet: the record ends in "+all" (or a bare "all"), or includes a record that does. "?all" and a missing "all" are weaker problems: they make SPF neutral for unlisted senders, so it never fails.

**How to fix:** End the record with "-all" (or "~all" while rolling out) and remove includes of records that end in +all.

**References:**

- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7208#section-5.1>

## email.spf.syntax

**Invalid SPF record** · passive · default severity **high**

The SPF record, or a record it includes or redirects to, is malformed or cannot be evaluated. Receivers treat this as a permanent error and SPF stops protecting the domain.

**How to fix:** Fix the reported term. Included domains must publish exactly one valid SPF record.

**References:**

- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7208#section-4.6>
- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7208#section-5.2>

## email.spf.void_lookups

**SPF has too many void lookups** · passive · default severity **medium**

More than two DNS lookups made while evaluating SPF return no records. RFC 7208 lets receivers fail evaluation after two, so stale includes and a/mx terms for deleted hosts can break SPF.

**How to fix:** Remove terms that point at names which no longer exist or have no records.

**References:**

- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7208#section-4.6.4>

## email.starttls.cert_expiring

**MX host TLS certificate expires soon** · active · default severity **medium**

An MX host's otherwise valid certificate expires within 21 days (7 days: high). Renewal automation often covers the web server but not the mail server.

**How to fix:** Renew the certificate and make sure the mail server reloads it; automate both steps.

**References:**

- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3207>
- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8461>

## email.starttls.cert_invalid

**MX host has an invalid TLS certificate** · active · default severity **medium**

An MX host's certificate is expired, not issued for its host name, or not signed by a trusted authority. Senders enforcing MTA-STS or DANE refuse to deliver, and others can't tell the real server from an impostor.

**How to fix:** Install a certificate from a public CA (e.g. Let's Encrypt) covering the MX host name, with the full intermediate chain.

**References:**

- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3207>
- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8461>

## email.starttls.unsupported

**MX host does not support STARTTLS** · active · default severity **high**

An MX host doesn't advertise STARTTLS, or fails the TLS handshake after advertising it. Mail to it travels in plaintext, readable by anyone on the network path.

**How to fix:** Enable STARTTLS on the mail server with a certificate for its host name.

**References:**

- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3207>
- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8461>

## email.tlsrpt.missing

**No TLS-RPT record** · passive · default severity **low**

The domain publishes no valid TLS reporting record at _smtp._tls, so sending servers have nowhere to report TLS failures delivering to you. You won't learn that MTA-STS or STARTTLS is broken until mail stops arriving.

**How to fix:** Publish "_smtp._tls TXT v=TLSRPTv1; rua=mailto:tlsrpt@&lt;domain&gt;".

**References:**

- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8460#section-3>
